topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Applying Pythagoras' theorem
topic.description: Apply Pythagoras’ Theorem (a² + b² = c²) to calculate unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles, including in real-world and coordinate-geometry contexts
evidence: Calculate the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle given the two shorter sides
Find a shorter side given the hypotenuse and the other short side
Use Pythagoras’ Theorem to find the distance between two points on a coordinate grid
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to check whether a shelf bracket makes a perfect right angle and the sides measure 30 cm, 40 cm, and 50 cm, can they use Pythagoras to verify?

pedagogy.summary: Pythagoras' Theorem (a²+b²=c²) lets pupils find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle. Experts see one step; novices experience many (Barton): identify the hypotenuse, decide whether Pythagoras applies, recall the relationship, decide square-and-ADD (finding the hypotenuse) vs square-and-SUBTRACT (finding a shorter side), substitute, and take the square root. The load-bearing obstacle is identifying the hypotenuse by POSITION (opposite the right angle, always the longest side) rather than by its number — and then letting that identification choose the operation. A side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle, not because of the digits on it (Foster).
bestPractices: Label the hypotenuse FIRST, before any calculation, using its two-part identity: opposite the right angle AND the longest side — then let that decide add vs subtract
Vary triangle orientation deliberately and use non-examples: pupils circle the hypotenuse across triangles rotated every which way so they don't default to 'the missing side is always c'
Contrast tasks where the SAME numeric length is a leg in one triangle and the hypotenuse in another (Foster), breaking the habit of judging by the number
Separate the two question types explicitly — 'find the hypotenuse' (square and add) vs 'find a shorter side' (square and subtract) — and practise switching between them
Build in a reasonableness check tied to the hypotenuse's identity: the hypotenuse must be the longest side, so a hypotenuse of 25 for legs 3 and 4 is impossible
For coordinate distance, draw the horizontal and vertical legs explicitly so the segment between the points is seen as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle
keyRepresentations: The three squares on the three sides — the two smaller squares' areas summing to the largest (area-dissection proof)
A right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse circled (opposite the right angle) before any numbers are used
Coordinate grid with the horizontal and vertical legs drawn between two points and the connecting segment as the hypotenuse
Side-by-side triangles where one shared length is a leg in one and a hypotenuse in the other
commonMisconceptions: Assumes the unknown side is always the hypotenuse, so always squares and ADDS — even when asked for a shorter side (the most common error; often triggered by triangle orientation)
Muddles a hypotenuse with a leg — judges by the number rather than by which side is opposite the right angle
When finding a shorter side, subtracts the wrong way around (leg² − hypotenuse² instead of hypotenuse² − leg²)
Forgets the final square root, reporting the squared value (e.g. 25 instead of 5)
For coordinate distance, adds the horizontal and vertical differences (3+4=7) or counts diagonal grid squares instead of forming a right triangle and applying the theorem

learn.summary: Teaches pupils to apply Pythagoras' Theorem (a²+b²=c²) to find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle, including on a coordinate grid. The load-bearing move is identifying the hypotenuse by POSITION (opposite the right angle, always the longest side) — not by its digits — and then letting whether the hypotenuse is known or unknown decide square-and-ADD (finding the hypotenuse) vs square-and-SUBTRACT, hypotenuse²−leg² (finding a shorter side). Experts see one step; novices experience many: identify the hypotenuse, decide whether Pythagoras applies, recall the relationship, choose add vs subtract, substitute, and take the square root.

activities.title: Pour the squares: seeing a²+b²=c²
feedback: If the two smaller squares exactly tile the largest, confirm: 'The areas on the two shorter sides add up to the area on the longest side — that is a²+b²=c².'
As the legs are dragged, keep the live readout visible so pupils see the relationship hold for every triangle, not just one.
Reinforce that the largest square always sits on the side opposite the right angle (the hypotenuse).
activities.rationale: Grounding the symbolic relationship in an area-dissection the pupil can recompute makes a²+b²=c² meaningful before it is used procedurally. Live recomputation (dragging legs, pouring tiles, updating readout) lets the relationship be seen as true rather than told.
learnerActions: Drag the two legs of a right-angled triangle and watch a square inflate on each of the three sides.
Watch the two smaller squares dissolve and tile, piece by piece, into the big square on the longest side, filling it exactly.
Read a live readout that updates to show a²+b²=c² as the legs change.
Optionally tap each square to reveal its area and confirm the two smaller areas sum to the largest.
activities.intendedInsight: The theorem is a relationship between the areas of the squares on the three sides: the two smaller squares together exactly fill the square on the hypotenuse, so a²+b² IS c² rather than a formula to memorise.

activities.title: Circle the hypotenuse first, then choose add or subtract
feedback: If a pupil picks 'add' for a shorter-side question, show the square built on their computed leg visibly overflow the hypotenuse square to force the rethink, then prompt: 'If this is bigger than the hypotenuse, something is wrong — the hypotenuse must be the longest side.'
If the hypotenuse is misidentified on a rotated triangle, point back to the right angle: 'The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle — find the right angle first.'

If a pupil subtracts leg²−hypotenuse² and gets a negative/nonsense value, anchor on the identity: the hypotenuse's square is the TOTAL, so a missing leg is hypotenuse²−leg² (rearranging c²=a²+b² to a²=c²−b²).

If a pupil reports the squared value as the length (e.g. 144 for a triangle with hypotenuse 13 and leg 5, since 13²−5²=144), prompt the last step and reasonableness: '144 is larger than the hypotenuse 13, so it cannot be a shorter side — take the square root to get the length (√144 = 12).'
On the paired-triangle task, confirm: 'The 10 is a hypotenuse here because it is opposite the right angle, and a leg there — the number alone does not decide.'
activities.rationale: The most common error is reflexively squaring-and-adding for every triangle, often triggered by orientation; forcing hypotenuse identification by position before the operation unlocks, and contrasting triangles where the same number plays different roles, directly targets both the always-add error and judging by digits. Separating 'find the hypotenuse' from 'find a shorter side' makes the add-vs-subtract decision explicit, and a longest-side reasonableness check catches add-when-should-subtract and the missing square root.
sourceClaims: On a diagnostic item asking for a SHORTER side, the most popular wrong answer came from pupils who failed to realise they were not being asked for the hypotenuse and applied a²+b²=c² by adding the two given sides (attributed partly to triangle orientation); another wrong answer subtracted the wrong way around (smaller minus larger); another had the correct subtraction but forgot to take the square root. Pythagoras is a multi-step process for novices: identify the hypotenuse, decide if Pythagoras applies, recall the formula, rearrange, substitute, calculate, interpret.

Pupils often muddle up calculating a hypotenuse with calculating a leg; the same numeric length can be a leg in one triangle and a hypotenuse in another, so a side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle, not because of its number (a 10 cm side must be the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle). Teachers should watch for pupils being unsure whether to square-and-add or square-and-subtract, which depends on whether the unknown is the hypotenuse or a leg.
learnerActions: On right-angled triangles drawn in varied orientations (none with the right angle at the bottom-left), tap or circle the hypotenuse — accepted only when it is the side opposite the right angle, not the longest-looking one on the page.
For each triangle, state whether the hypotenuse is the KNOWN side or the UNKNOWN side before choosing an operation.
Choose square-and-ADD when the unknown side is the hypotenuse; choose square-and-SUBTRACT (hypotenuse²−leg²) when the unknown is a shorter side.
Compare two side-by-side triangles where the same numeric length (e.g. 10) is a leg in one and the hypotenuse in the other, and label each correctly.
Finish each calculation by taking the square root, then check the hypotenuse is the longest side.
activities.intendedInsight: A side is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle (and so the longest), not because of its digits; which side is unknown — not the size of the numbers — decides whether you add or subtract.

activities.title: Distance between two points as a hypotenuse
feedback: If a pupil adds the differences (e.g. 4+3=7), prompt: 'Adding the two leg lengths does not give the hypotenuse — square each, add, then take the square root: √(4²+3²)=√25=5.'
If a pupil counts diagonal grid squares along the sloping line, redraw the horizontal and vertical legs and return to the right-triangle picture.
Confirm the method transfers: 'You built the right triangle from the coordinate differences — the same move works for any two points.'
activities.rationale: Coordinate distance is a real-world/geometry application, and the characteristic errors (adding differences, counting diagonal squares) come from not forming a right triangle. Drawing the legs explicitly between draggable points keeps it as a Pythagoras problem rather than a new formula to memorise.
learnerActions: Plot two points on a coordinate grid (e.g. (1,2) and (5,5)).
Draw the horizontal and vertical legs between the points explicitly, so the connecting segment is seen as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle.
Find the horizontal difference (Δx) and vertical difference (Δy), then compute distance = √(Δx²+Δy²).
Try a second pair of points unprompted, constructing the right triangle yourself before calculating.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding the straight-line distance between two points is a Pythagoras problem: the segment between them is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical differences.

constraints: Pupils must identify the hypotenuse by position (opposite the right angle) before choosing an operation; do not let the activity accept the longest-looking side on the page or let the add/subtract choice precede this identification.
Vary triangle orientation deliberately, including right angles not at the bottom-left, so pupils do not default to 'the missing side is always c'.
Every calculation must end with a square root and a longest-side reasonableness check (a shorter side cannot exceed the hypotenuse), to catch the un-rooted value and add-when-should-subtract errors.

A static tap-to-reveal card can present the area-square proof and the two-part hypotenuse identity, but it cannot recompute as the triangle changes, so the add-vs-subtract decision stays told rather than practised — treat it as a summary scaffold, not the main task.

A recognition-only quiz (which side is the hypotenuse? add or subtract? fill the blank, plus a coordinate item with a 4+3=7 distractor) can reliably score the method-choice in fixed steps, but does not itself let the pupil see the leg-squares fill the hypotenuse square or construct the right triangle themselves.

A spoken/in-role character can pose problems verbally but does not itself render the area relationship or the coordinate legs the pupil must produce and see; keep the discriminating evidence as a computed length and a correctly identified hypotenuse.
3D space-diagonal work (√(a²+b²+c²)) is a later extension beyond this topic's add-vs-subtract objective; reserve it rather than including it here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the teaching principle, not the efficacy of any specific activity.

Self-audit of worked values (all consistent with the source): √(6²+8²)=√100=10; √(13²−5²)=√144=12; √(4²+3²)=√25=5 for the (1,2)→(5,5) distance (Δx=4, Δy=3). These check out and were kept in feedback/examples.

The source claim that '3D adds nothing to the core insight' is a catalog-style comparison; it has been softened to a scoped statement that 3D space-diagonals are a later extension beyond this topic, not a universal claim about 3D's value.

Claims that a static image 'cannot practise' the decision and that a conversation 'cannot render' the relationship were softened to narrowly-scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints rather than asserted as universal laws.

The National Curriculum coordinate-grid claim is marked verified:false in the source row; it establishes that coordinate-grid Pythagoras is in KS3 scope but does not support the specific teaching principle of the coordinate activity, so it is retained here as scope context rather than cited as a sourceClaim.

In any right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is strictly the longest side, so 'opposite the right angle' and 'longest side' never conflict, including near-isosceles cases; flagged only for reviewer awareness.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the hypotenuse on this one' — then rotate the triangle 130° and ask again; does the pupil track it by position (opposite the right angle) or lose it?

Counterexample: 'Here is a triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13. If I tell you the answer for the missing side came out bigger than 13, what has gone wrong?' (the hypotenuse must be the longest — flushes out add-when-should-subtract).
'You added for triangle A and subtracted for triangle B — how did each triangle tell you which to do?' (checks the decision is driven by which side is unknown, not guessed).
'Without a triangle drawn, find the distance from (2,1) to (7,13). What right-angled triangle are you using?' (checks they can construct the legs from coordinates themselves).
assess.correctAnswer: (1) The hypotenuse is circled as the side opposite the right angle on every triangle, regardless of orientation. (2) √(6²+8²)=√100=10 cm (square and add — finding the hypotenuse). (3) √(13²−5²)=√144=12 cm (square and subtract — finding a shorter side, hypotenuse² minus leg²). (4) Horizontal leg 4, vertical leg 3, distance √(4²+3²)=√25=5 (forms a right triangle from the coordinate differences).

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the unknown is always the hypotenuse, so squares and ADDS every time: 'a²+b²=c², so I add the two numbers' — even when asked for a shorter side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the pupil circle the hypotenuse FIRST (opposite the right angle, longest side) and state whether it is known or unknown before choosing the operation: unknown hypotenuse → add; unknown leg → subtract. Contrast triangles where the same length is a leg in one and the hypotenuse in another. Reteach right-angle/triangle-property identification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 adds 13²+5² and roots (≈13.9) instead of subtracting; may misidentify the hypotenuse on the rotated triangles in task 1; the orientation of the triangle often triggers the default

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the wrong way around when finding a shorter side: computes leg² − hypotenuse² (smaller minus larger) because 'it's the smaller side so put the smaller number first'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on the identity a²+b²=c²: the hypotenuse is the largest, so its square is the TOTAL; a missing leg is total minus the other leg's square, hypotenuse² − leg². Rearranging c²=a²+b² to a²=c²−b² is the formula move to reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 writes 5²−13² and gets a negative or nonsense value; the operation type (subtract) is right but the order is reversed

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the final square root, reporting the squared value as the length (e.g. gives 100 or 144 instead of 10 or 12)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: add a routine last step and a reasonableness check — the hypotenuse must be the longest side, so 144 for these lengths is impossible; the answer must be re-rooted. Have the pupil sketch and sanity-check magnitude.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes the correct squared expression (13²−5²=144) then stops, or gives the un-rooted number as the answer

errorPatterns.pattern: For coordinate distance, adds the horizontal and vertical differences (4+3=7) or counts diagonal grid squares instead of forming a right triangle and applying the theorem
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: draw the horizontal and vertical legs between the two points explicitly; the connecting segment is the hypotenuse, so distance = √(Δx²+Δy²). Return to the right-triangle picture rather than treating it as a new formula.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 4 gives 7, or counts squares along the sloping line; does not draw the horizontal and vertical legs

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably identify the hypotenuse once the triangle is rotated; squares and adds on every task, including the shorter-side question; or adds coordinate differences. Treats a²+b²=c² as 'add the two numbers'.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the hypotenuse by position in any orientation; chooses square-and-add for an unknown hypotenuse and square-and-subtract (hypotenuse² − leg², correct order) for an unknown leg; square-roots and sanity-checks that the hypotenuse is longest; and constructs a right triangle from coordinate differences to find distance, transferring the method to a new pair unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the hypotenuse correctly and squares-and-adds (task 2), but stumbles on the shorter-side case — subtracts the wrong way, reverts to adding, or omits the square root — or cannot form the right triangle for the coordinate distance. Lists the steps but does not let 'which side is unknown' govern add vs subtract.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the pupil three right-angled triangles drawn in DIFFERENT orientations (none with the right angle at the bottom-left) plus a coordinate grid, and set four tasks to WATCH them do — do not explain first: (1) On each triangle, circle the hypotenuse. (2) Triangle A has the two shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm — find the third side. (3) Triangle B has hypotenuse 13 cm and one shorter side 5 cm — find the other shorter side. (4) Plot the points (1,2) and (5,5) and find the straight-line distance between them. Watch how they identify the hypotenuse, whether they add or subtract, and whether they finish with a square root.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The set forces the discriminating decisions the theorem depends on. Varied orientation exposes whoever identifies the hypotenuse by look or position-on-the-page rather than 'opposite the right angle'. Task 3 (a shorter-side question) separates pupils who square-and-subtract from those who reflexively square-and-add for every triangle. Task 4 separates pupils who form a right triangle from the coordinate differences from those who add the differences or count diagonal squares. A pupil who mechanically adds and roots will succeed on 2 but fail 3 — the tell.

topic.name: Trigonometry basics
topic.description: Use the trigonometric ratios sin, cos, and tan in right-angled triangles to find unknown sides and angles, including setting up the correct ratio for a given problem
evidence: Identify which trigonometric ratio to use (SOH CAH TOA) based on the known and unknown sides
Calculate an unknown side using sin, cos, or tan and a known angle
Find an unknown angle using the inverse trigonometric function (e.g. tan⁻¹)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a ladder is 5 metres long and leans against a wall at 70° to the ground, can they use trigonometry to work out how high up the wall it reaches?

pedagogy.summary: Right-angled trigonometry (sin, cos, tan) extends Pythagoras by relating an ANGLE to a pair of sides. The two shorter sides are named RELATIVE TO THE REFERENCE ANGLE θ — opposite is across from θ, adjacent is next to θ — while only the hypotenuse is fixed by the right angle (NCETM). The central danger is that pupils reduce trigonometry to procedural mnemonic use (SOHCAHTOA) without understanding, so they mislabel the sides, pick the wrong ratio, and cannot recover when a triangle is rotated. NCETM roots the ratios in similarity and the unit circle: for a given angle the ratio of two sides is invariant regardless of the triangle's size (the 'within-triangle' ratio), and that constant IS sin/cos/tan of the angle.
bestPractices: Mark the reference angle θ FIRST, then label opposite (across from θ) and adjacent (next to θ, and NOT the hypotenuse) relative to it — never relative to the right angle
Show explicitly that opposite and adjacent SWAP when you switch to the other acute angle, while the hypotenuse stays put — so the labels depend on which angle you are working from

Ground the ratios in similarity/ratio-invariance before the mnemonic: for a fixed angle, opposite÷hypotenuse is the same across nested similar triangles (NCETM's unit-circle and scale-factor route), so the ratio has meaning, not just letters
Sequence problem-solving: identify the two sides involved (one known, one unknown), then choose the single ratio that contains exactly those two sides
Distinguish the two problem types — unknown SIDE (rearrange the ratio, e.g. o = h·sinθ) vs unknown ANGLE (apply the inverse function, e.g. θ = tan⁻¹(o/a))
Start in a standard orientation to keep the unit-circle link visible, then deliberately rotate triangles once the naming convention is secure
Reasonableness checks: the hypotenuse is the longest side, and an acute angle in a right triangle is between 0° and 90°
keyRepresentations: A right triangle with a movable reference-angle marker θ, and opposite/adjacent labels that re-attach as θ moves
The unit circle with the rotating radius, showing sinθ as the y-coordinate and cosθ as the x-coordinate
Nested similar right triangles showing opposite÷hypotenuse constant for a fixed angle (ratio invariance)
SOH-CAH-TOA presented as three side-pairs, each ratio highlighting exactly the two sides it uses
commonMisconceptions: Labels opposite and adjacent relative to the RIGHT angle instead of the reference angle θ, so every ratio is set up wrong
Relies on the SOHCAHTOA mnemonic without understanding, and cannot choose which ratio applies when given a particular pair of sides
Mislabels the sides when the triangle is drawn rotated or in a non-standard orientation
For an unknown side, cannot rearrange the ratio to isolate it (e.g. leaves the unknown in the denominator)
For an unknown angle, forgets to use the inverse function (uses sin instead of sin⁻¹) or reports the ratio value as if it were the angle

learn.summary: Right-angled trigonometry (sin, cos, tan) relates a reference angle θ to a pair of sides. The two shorter sides are named RELATIVE TO θ — opposite is across from θ, adjacent is next to θ — while only the hypotenuse is fixed (opposite the right angle, longest side). The central danger is reducing trigonometry to mnemonic recitation (SOHCAHTOA) without understanding, so learners mislabel sides, pick the wrong ratio and cannot recover when a triangle is rotated or when they work from the other acute angle. Ground the ratios in similarity/ratio-invariance: for a fixed angle the within-triangle ratio (e.g. opposite÷hypotenuse) is constant across similar triangles, and that constant IS sin of the angle. Distinguish finding an unknown SIDE (rearrange the ratio) from finding an unknown ANGLE (apply the inverse function).

activities.title: Labels that move with the reference angle
feedback: If a learner picks 'adjacent' by looking at the right angle instead of at θ (both shorter sides touch the right angle, so that cannot decide it), insist on marking θ first: adjacent is the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse, opposite is across from θ, and neither is the hypotenuse.
If opposite and adjacent do NOT swap when θ moves to the other acute angle, this signals labelling relative to the right angle rather than θ — demonstrate the swap explicitly by moving θ.
If the hypotenuse is identified unreliably in a rotated triangle, reteach it as the side opposite the right angle (the Pythagoras prerequisite).
activities.rationale: The reference-angle dependence is the first conceptual hinge and a known failure point; naming relative to the right angle sets up every subsequent ratio wrong. The swap when switching acute angles makes the convention discoverable rather than recited.
sourceClaims: Opposite and adjacent are defined relative to a given (reference) angle — adjacent is the side next to a given angle, opposite is the side opposite a given angle — while the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Pupils may rely on mnemonics such as SOHCAHTOA without understanding, reducing trigonometry to procedural formula application, and may struggle to know which ratio to apply. The multiplier changes as the angle changes; a standard orientation is used initially to keep the unit-circle link. For a given angle the within-triangle ratio is invariant across similar triangles (opposite÷hypotenuse constant = sin of the angle), connecting trigonometry to similarity and scale factor.
learnerActions: Mark the reference angle θ FIRST on a right-angled triangle, then label 'opposite' (across from θ) and 'adjacent' (next to θ, and NOT the hypotenuse) relative to it.
Label the hypotenuse as the side opposite the right angle — the longest side, which stays fixed.
Now mark the OTHER acute angle as θ on the same triangle and relabel: notice opposite and adjacent SWAP places while the hypotenuse stays put.
Repeat on a triangle drawn rotated out of standard orientation, labelling relative to θ rather than to the shape.
If a draggable θ marker is available, drag θ between the two acute vertices and watch the opposite/adjacent labels re-attach and swap live while the hypotenuse label stays fixed.
activities.intendedInsight: Opposite and adjacent are not glued to the shape; they depend on which angle you are working from. Only the hypotenuse is fixed by the right angle.

activities.title: The ratio that refuses to change (similarity before the mnemonic)
feedback: If a learner expects sin θ to grow when the triangle is enlarged, point to the table: the lengths grew together, so their ratio is unchanged.
Reconnect the constant to similarity and scale factor: similar triangles share side ratios, which is why the angle alone determines the ratio.
Ask the counterexample probe: 'You doubled the triangle but kept the angle. Does sin θ change? Why or why not?'
activities.rationale: Ratio-invariance is the second conceptual hinge and distinguishes understanding from memorisation; rooting sin/cos/tan in similarity gives the mnemonic meaning. The constant-value demonstration is only felt when values are compared across sizes.
sourceClaims: Opposite and adjacent are defined relative to a given (reference) angle — adjacent is the side next to a given angle, opposite is the side opposite a given angle — while the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Pupils may rely on mnemonics such as SOHCAHTOA without understanding, reducing trigonometry to procedural formula application, and may struggle to know which ratio to apply. The multiplier changes as the angle changes; a standard orientation is used initially to keep the unit-circle link. For a given angle the within-triangle ratio is invariant across similar triangles (opposite÷hypotenuse constant = sin of the angle), connecting trigonometry to similarity and scale factor.
learnerActions: Keep the angle θ fixed and scale a right-angled triangle bigger and smaller (nested similar triangles).
For each size, measure or read opposite and hypotenuse and compute opposite÷hypotenuse; record the values in a table.
Confirm the ratio stays constant (for example 0.42 at every size when θ = 25°) even though the side lengths all change.
Connect this constant to a unit-circle inset: it is named sin θ (with sin θ as the y-coordinate and cos θ as the x-coordinate of the rotating radius).
If a live-scaling model is available, drag to resize the triangle and watch a readout of opp÷hyp stay fixed while the lengths change, with the unit-circle inset naming the constant.
activities.intendedInsight: For a given angle the ratio of two sides is invariant regardless of the triangle's size, and that constant value IS sin/cos/tan of the angle — so the ratio has meaning, not just letters.

activities.title: Choose the ratio, then solve for a side or an angle
feedback: If a learner recites SOHCAHTOA but cannot pick a ratio, have them name the two sides involved first, then find the one ratio containing exactly those two (opposite and adjacent → tan, not sin).
If for an unknown side they compute 10÷sin 35° or sin 35°÷10 instead of 10×sin 35°, treat it as a change-of-subject step: when the unknown is the numerator, o = h × sin θ.
If for an unknown angle they report 0.75 as the angle or compute tan(0.75), flag the question type — the unknown is an ANGLE, so apply the inverse function to the ratio.
Reasonableness checks: reject any answer where a shorter side exceeds the hypotenuse, or an acute angle falls outside 0°–90°.
activities.rationale: Separating side-problems from angle-problems targets two distinct documented errors (failure to rearrange, and forgetting the inverse). Grounding ratio choice in the side pair rather than the mnemonic addresses the core 'procedure without understanding' risk. The objective's scope covers using the ratios to find both unknown sides and unknown angles.
sourceClaims: Opposite and adjacent are defined relative to a given (reference) angle — adjacent is the side next to a given angle, opposite is the side opposite a given angle — while the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Pupils may rely on mnemonics such as SOHCAHTOA without understanding, reducing trigonometry to procedural formula application, and may struggle to know which ratio to apply. The multiplier changes as the angle changes; a standard orientation is used initially to keep the unit-circle link. For a given angle the within-triangle ratio is invariant across similar triangles (opposite÷hypotenuse constant = sin of the angle), connecting trigonometry to similarity and scale factor.
learnerActions: Given a problem, identify the two sides involved — one known, one unknown — relative to the marked angle θ.
Choose the single ratio (SOH, CAH or TOA) that contains exactly those two sides.
For an unknown SIDE: rearrange the ratio to make the unknown the subject, e.g. from sin 35° = o/10 derive o = 10 × sin 35° ≈ 5.74 cm. (Check: the opposite side cannot exceed the hypotenuse.)
For an unknown ANGLE: apply the inverse function, e.g. from tan θ = 6/8 (opposite 6, adjacent 8) derive θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°. (Check: an acute angle lies between 0° and 90°.)
Practise a worked case where adjacent and hypotenuse are known: use cosine, θ = cos⁻¹(adjacent/hypotenuse).
If a guided problem mode is available, let it highlight the two relevant sides and branch between 'find a side' (rearrange) and 'find the angle' (inverse).
activities.intendedInsight: Ratio selection follows from the pair of sides involved; and whether you rearrange or invert depends on whether the unknown is a side or an angle.

activities.title: Check and discriminate (fixed-step assessment)
feedback: Correct ratio selection can be scored reliably, but fixed-step items check the end states, not whether the learner can see the labels swap or the ratio stay constant — pair with the interactive labelling and scaling activities.
Flag items where a shorter-side (leg) answer is not less than the hypotenuse, a hypotenuse answer is not greater than the known leg, or an acute-angle answer does not lie strictly between 0° and 90°.
activities.rationale: Discrete-step items discriminate well across the sub-skills and surface each error pattern, but recognition-style responses do not elicit independent construction of the labelled triangle or demonstrate the sense of invariance, so they complement rather than replace the exploratory tasks.
learnerActions: Match 'opposite', 'adjacent' and 'hypotenuse' to a triangle with θ marked; then re-answer with θ on the OTHER acute angle to show the swap.
Given two sides, select which ratio applies.
Fill in the blank to compute an unknown side from a known angle.
Fill in the blank using the inverse function (e.g. tan⁻¹) to find an unknown angle.
Include at least one rotated (non-standard orientation) triangle among the items.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm that labels anchor to the reference angle, the correct ratio is chosen for a given side pair, and side-vs-angle problems are finished correctly.

constraints: Mark the reference angle θ FIRST; always label opposite/adjacent relative to θ, never relative to the right angle. Only the hypotenuse is fixed (opposite the right angle, longest side).
Introduce ratio-invariance and similarity BEFORE the SOHCAHTOA mnemonic, so the ratio has meaning rather than being spelled.
Start in a standard orientation to keep the unit-circle link visible, then deliberately rotate triangles once the naming convention is secure.
Keep the two problem types explicitly distinct: unknown SIDE → rearrange the ratio; unknown ANGLE → apply the inverse function.
Apply reasonableness checks: a shorter side is never longer than the hypotenuse; an acute angle lies between 0° and 90°.

A tap-to-reveal / static labelled triangle can serve as a summary card (reveal opposite/adjacent relative to θ, reveal the hypotenuse as 'opposite the right angle, longest, unchanged', and name which two sides each ratio uses), but it cannot recompute, so the swap and the invariance remain told rather than shown — use it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the dynamic or constructive work.
Fixed-step/recognition items assess end states and do not require the learner to independently construct the labelled triangle or demonstrate the ratio staying constant.
Prerequisites to reteach when they surface: reliably identifying the hypotenuse (Pythagoras skill) and rearranging formulae (change of subject).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of worked examples: sin 35° × 10 ≈ 5.736 ≈ 5.74 cm (correct); tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.87° ≈ 36.9° (correct); sin 25° ≈ 0.4226 ≈ 0.42 (correct). All examples preserved as given.

The original catalog claims that a 3D environment 'adds nothing' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot render' the swapping labels were fit judgements, not established efficacy findings; they are reframed as narrowly-scoped medium notes (these media cannot dynamically recompute the swap or invariance), not asserted as universal limits. The content IS planar, so 2D representation is natural, but no claim is made that other media cannot teach it.

The National Curriculum source (gov.uk) is marked verified:false in the row and is a curriculum-scope statement; it has been removed from Activity 3 sourceClaims and is retained only as objective-scope context (that both unknown-side and unknown-angle problems are in scope), not as support for the specific pedagogical approach.

The unit-circle convention (sin = y-coordinate, cos = x-coordinate) is standard but presented here as a representational aid; confirm the intended age-group framing (ages 13–15) is appropriate before leading with the unit circle versus similarity.

probeDeeper: 'Point to θ. Now which side is opposite? ... Now suppose we work from the OTHER acute angle instead — which side is opposite now?' (checks the labels are anchored to the reference angle, not the shape).
Counterexample: 'You made this triangle twice as big but kept the angle the same. Does sin θ change? Why or why not?' (checks ratio invariance is understood, not memorised).
'This one asks for a side and that one asks for an angle — how does each tell you whether to rearrange the ratio or use the inverse function?' (checks the side-vs-angle decision).
'Your answer for the opposite side came out longer than the hypotenuse. Is that possible?' (reasonableness check on magnitude).
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Opposite = across from θ, adjacent = next to θ, hypotenuse = opposite the right angle; when the reference angle switches to the other acute angle, opposite and adjacent SWAP while the hypotenuse is unchanged. (2) sin35° = o/10, so o = 10×sin35° ≈ 5.74 cm (rearrange the ratio). (3) tanθ = 6/8, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9° (inverse function). (4) Adjacent and hypotenuse → cosine; θ = cos⁻¹(adjacent/hypotenuse).

errorPatterns.pattern: Labels opposite and adjacent relative to the RIGHT angle rather than the reference angle θ, so the sides are named wrong before any ratio is chosen
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on marking θ first, then opposite = across from θ, adjacent = next to θ (not the hypotenuse); demonstrate the swap by moving θ to the other acute angle. If the hypotenuse itself is unreliable in rotated triangles, reteach identifying it as the side opposite the right angle (the Pythagoras skill).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 1 marks the side next to the right angle as 'adjacent'; does not swap opposite and adjacent when θ moves to the other acute angle; may be unable to identify the hypotenuse reliably on the rotated triangle

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on the SOHCAHTOA mnemonic without understanding and cannot choose which ratio applies to a given pair of sides
errorPatterns.nextMove: Root the choice in meaning: identify the two sides involved (known + unknown), then select the single ratio containing exactly those two. Reconnect to the unit circle / similarity so the ratio is understood, not just spelled.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recites SOH CAH TOA but on tasks 3/4 cannot pick the ratio that contains exactly the two sides involved; may use sin when the two sides are opposite and adjacent (should be tan)

errorPatterns.pattern: For an unknown SIDE, cannot rearrange the ratio to isolate it — leaves the unknown in the denominator or divides the wrong way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat as a change-of-subject step: o = h×sinθ when the unknown is the numerator; practise rearranging the three ratio forms. Reteach formula rearrangement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 writes sin35°=o/10 but then computes 10÷sin35° or sin35°÷10 instead of 10×sin35°; cannot make the unknown the subject

errorPatterns.pattern: For an unknown ANGLE, forgets the inverse function — uses sin/tan instead of sin⁻¹/tan⁻¹, or reports the ratio value as the angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: flag the question type ('the unknown is an ANGLE') and pair each direct function with its inverse — ratio→angle needs the inverse. Add a reasonableness check that the angle is between 0° and 90°.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 gives 0.75 or computes tan(0.75) instead of tan⁻¹(0.75); has the ratio set up correctly but does not invert to recover the angle

responseLevels.gap: Labels opposite/adjacent from the right angle (does not swap when θ moves); recites SOHCAHTOA but cannot select a ratio for a given side pair; cannot set up or finish either a side or an angle problem.
responseLevels.full: Labels opposite and adjacent relative to the reference angle in any orientation (and swaps them correctly when the angle moves); selects the ratio containing the two relevant sides; rearranges to find an unknown side and uses the inverse function to find an unknown angle; sanity-checks that the hypotenuse is longest and the angle is between 0° and 90°, transferring the method to a fresh triangle unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Labels and picks a ratio in a standard-orientation triangle and finds an unknown SIDE, but mislabels when the triangle is rotated or when θ switches to the other acute angle, and/or cannot find an unknown ANGLE — omits the inverse function or reports the ratio as the angle. Lists the mnemonic without letting the reference angle govern the labels.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the pupil right-angled triangles with a reference angle θ marked (draw at least one rotated out of standard orientation), and set four tasks to WATCH — do not explain first: (1) On a triangle with θ marked, label the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse; then, on the SAME triangle, mark the other acute angle and label opposite and adjacent for THAT angle. (2) A triangle has θ=35° and hypotenuse 10 cm — find the side opposite θ. (3) A triangle has the two shorter sides 6 cm (opposite) and 8 cm (adjacent) — find angle θ. (4) A triangle gives you the adjacent side and the hypotenuse and asks for the angle — which ratio do you use, and how do you finish? Watch how they label relative to the angle, which ratio they pick, and whether they rearrange or use an inverse.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task 1's second half is the hinge: a pupil who labels relative to the reference angle will swap opposite and adjacent when the angle moves; a pupil who labels relative to the RIGHT angle will leave them unchanged. Task 3 (unknown angle) separates pupils who reach for the inverse function from those who compute sin(6/8) or report the ratio 0.75 as the angle. Tasks 2 vs 3 separate 'unknown side → rearrange' from 'unknown angle → inverse'. A pupil who merely recites SOHCAHTOA will label and recite but stall on choosing and finishing.

sources.claim: Opposite and adjacent are defined relative to a given (reference) angle — adjacent is the side next to a given angle, opposite is the side opposite a given angle — while the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Pupils may rely on mnemonics such as SOHCAHTOA without understanding, reducing trigonometry to procedural formula application, and may struggle to know which ratio to apply. The multiplier changes as the angle changes; a standard orientation is used initially to keep the unit-circle link. For a given angle the within-triangle ratio is invariant across similar triangles (opposite÷hypotenuse constant = sin of the angle), connecting trigonometry to similarity and scale factor.
